item.title: UAC-0099 Is Now Hiding Malware Inside a Fake Notepad++ Plugin to Target Ukrainian Organizations
item.description:
UAC-0099, a Russia-aligned actor targeting Ukrainian 🇺🇦 organizations, now delivers MATCHBOIL.V2 via a trojanized Notepad++ plugin, with an anti-analysis loader that deliberately exhausts RAM and CPU if run without correct arguments.
- Phishing email carries an image attachment hiding a link-shortener URL, redirecting to EasySend[.]co where a ZIP drops a VBScript disguised as a PDF (double extension with trailing spaces, e.g. "Zavodskyi rayon.pdf .vbs"). The script opens a decoy PDF while fetching Evernote.zip in the background, a full Notepad++ 8.8.3 bundle including the malicious plugin NppExport.dll.
- NppExport.dll (LUNCHPOKE) runs at Notepad++ startup, uses a bundled winrar.exe to unpack a password-protected updater.rar, drops RemoteLibUpdater.exe and InitTest.dll to %PUBLIC%\Libraries\fFthY3-Ytrevc3w-ab3\, and copies schtasks.exe to %PUBLIC%\Wallpapers\Background.exe before creating scheduled task \W1n3r-U09oTy-Ap5\Updates running every three minutes.
- RemoteLibUpdater.exe is BURNYBEAR, a loader for InitTest.dll (MATCHBOIL.V2). If executed without the "setup nodisplay" arguments, BURNYBEAR deliberately spikes RAM and CPU, burning sandbox analysis and frustrating manual triage.
Hunt: flag Notepad++ processes loading unsigned DLLs from the plugins directory, any scheduled task executing from %PUBLIC%\Libraries, and schtasks.exe copied outside System32. Full advisory and IOCs from CERT-UA.

item.title: US Agencies Warn of Laundry Bear Campaign Targeting Unpatched Zimbra Servers
item.description:
Russian-warned APT Laundry Bear is actively exploiting CVE-2025-66376, a zero-click XSS flaw in Zimbra Collaboration Suite, using custom tooling to silently steal mailboxes at scale.
Key findings:
- CVE-2025-66376 is an XSS vulnerability exploited as a zero-day before patching and still under active exploitation. The attack triggers the moment a victim views the email in ZCS webmail, no clicks required (T1203). A Base64-encoded payload hides inside an SVG element's onload field, driven by CSS @import directives to execute malicious JavaScript.
- The custom tool Ulej handles exploitation and exfiltration. It runs multi-stage recon, enables IMAP via a SOAP ModifyPrefsRequest setting zimbraPrefImapEnabled to TRUE, creates application passwords, harvests 2FA codes, pulls 90 days of email, contacts, OAuth tokens, and browser-saved credentials, then ships everything over HTTPS and DNS to the Flowerbed backend.
- Initial emails are sent from previously compromised accounts (T1566) to boost credibility. Payloads use XOR encryption plus Base64 encoding (T1027.013, T1027.017) to evade basic controls.
- Laundry Bear registered lookalike Zimbra domains for C2 and data collection: mailnalysis[.]com, zimbrastat[.]com, zimbra-metadata[.]com, zmailanalytics[.]com, istc-cloud[.]com, emailanalytics.com[.]ua.
Patch ZCS immediately.

item.title: Why Digital Forensic Reports Don’t Survive Cross-Examination
item.description:
Forensic reports that can't survive cross-examination: three landmark cases show exactly how unvalidated tool output, ignored alternative explanations, and artifact-to-intent leaps destroy cases in court.
- Casey Anthony trial (2011): CacheBack parsed Firefox 2's "Mork" history database and returned 84 visits to sci-spot[.]com when the true count was 1, a bug the tool's own developer discovered after testifying. The raw database was never manually verified against the tool's output. The jury was never corrected. The DFIR lesson: if a visit count, timestamp, or file hash is load-bearing, open the underlying database yourself and confirm the tool read it right.
- Julie Amero case (2004-2007): The state's examiner called browser cache hits "access" without ruling out the adware networks addynamics[.]com and adrevolver[.]com, a machine running Windows 98 with expired AV and no pop-up blocker. Conviction was set aside after the state conceded the testimony was erroneous. Artifact presence proves machine behavior, not human intent.
- UK 🇬🇧 Post Office/Horizon scandal (1999-2015): 980+ prosecutions rested on accounting shortfalls from Fujitsu's Horizon system, accepted in court under a legal presumption of computer reliability. Internal error logs were never audited. Mr Justice Fraser's 2019 judgment found "bugs, errors and defects" capable of producing the very discrepancies used to prosecute people. Vendor size is not a reliability audit.

item.title: Russian-Linked Hackers Target Zimbra Users With Zero-Day Exploit
item.description:
LAUNDRY BEAR, a Russian 🇷🇺 state-linked APT, weaponized CVE-2025-66376 as a zero-day against Zimbra Collaboration Suite, stealing 90 days of email, credentials, 2FA tokens, and Global Address Lists from Western government and defense targets since July 2025.
Key findings:
- CVE-2025-66376 is a view-based exploit: a victim only needs to render a malicious email in ZCS Classic Webmail for the JavaScript payload to fire. No click required. The flaw stems from improper sanitization of CSS @import directives; the payload uses Base64 and XOR encoding to evade signature detection. Patched in ZCS 10.1.13 and 10.0.18, but exploitation predates the patch by months.
- The 12-stage payload (Ulej) harvests email address, environment info, 2FA codes, app passwords, saved passwords, the Global Address List, and archives the last 90 days of mail. Exfiltration runs over DNS and HTTPS to the Flowerbed framework: a Python/Docker stack with Catcher (aggregator), Nginx (HTTPS reverse proxy), Certbot, and Gardener containers.
- LAUNDRY BEAR identifies exposed ZCS infrastructure via port scanning and commercial datasets, then seeds phishing from compromised victim accounts, complicating sender-based detection. Targeted sectors: defense industrial base, government, energy, law enforcement, NGOs, media, and education.
Patch to ZCS 10.1.13 / 10.0.18 immediately. If patching is delayed, disable Classic Webmail.

item.title: US agencies update advisory on Iranian cyber campaign targeting internet-connected PLCs in critical infrastructure
item.description:
Iranian 🇮🇷 IRGC-affiliated actors expand PLC targeting to Rockwell, Schneider Electric, and Siemens devices across US 🇺🇸 critical infrastructure, disabling safety logic and alarm systems since at least March 2026.
- CyberAv3ngers (Shahid Kaveh Group), linked to Iran 🇮🇷's IRGC Cyber Electronic Command, accessed internet-exposed PLCs using legitimate vendor engineering software (Studio 5000, EcoStruxure Control Expert, TIA Portal) from leased third-party infrastructure. No zero-days used: just open ports 44818, 2222, 102, 502, and SSH via Dropbear on port 22 against misconfigured, internet-facing devices.
- Affected hardware includes Rockwell CompactLogix and Micro850, Schneider Electric BMX P34/Modicon M340, and Siemens S7-1200 PLCs across water and wastewater, energy, and government sectors. Actors downloaded malicious project files that modified Add-On Instructions (AOIs), deleted shutdown and alarm logic, and manipulated HMI/SCADA displays, causing operational disruption and financial loss.
- For incident responders: compare running PLC ladder logic against known-good backups before restoring. Verify backup project files are clean before redeployment. Review modem, HMI, and workstation logs for lateral movement. Reimage compromised devices.
Updated IOCs and MITRE ATT&CK technique mappings are in the advisory. Hunt for inbound connections on those OT ports from hosting-provider IP ranges.

item.title: DNS Poisoning Tactics Expand to Hospitality Wi-Fi
item.description:
APT28-linked tradecraft targets hotel and conference Wi-Fi gateways across the US 🇺🇸, India 🇮🇳, and Saudi Arabia 🇸🇦 to harvest Microsoft 365 credentials without touching a single endpoint, active since at least June 2026.
- Attackers gain admin access to captive portal appliances via exposed SSH, SNMP, or web consoles with weak credentials, then poison DNS for every guest on the network. Forged responses redirect login.microsoftonline[.]com queries to 38.146.28[.]75 and 31.57.243[.]154, serving Microsoft-impersonating pages at m365-owa[.]com, owa-ms365[.]com, ms365-live[.]com, and ms365-device[.]com, all registered via chikolimdrid[at]gmail[.]com.
- Hard-coded DNS like 8.8.8[.]8 does not protect victims: the gateway reads, forges, and returns the response before it reaches upstream resolvers. Only strict-mode DoH/DoT or a full-tunnel VPN stops the redirect. Opportunistic encrypted DNS falls back to plaintext and remains vulnerable.
- In roughly one-third of cases the attacker also poisoned WPAD, pushing a malicious PAC file via svchost WinHttpAutoProxySvc to proxy all Windows application traffic through attacker infrastructure, a technique not seen in prior FrostArmada reporting.
- On ms365-live[.]com, ReliaQuest observed device-code flow abuse: victims approve what looks like a routine auth prompt and unknowingly grant the attacker valid, MFA-satisfied OAuth tokens, no credential interception required.

item.title: Chaos ransomware deploys browser-based msaRAT to evade network detection
item.description:
Chaos ransomware's msaRAT routes C2 entirely through Chrome or Edge via Chrome DevTools Protocol, making attacker traffic invisible on the wire. The RAT process never touches the network directly.
- msaRAT is a Rust-based RAT attributed to the Chaos ransomware group. Initial access delivers update_ms.msi via curl over HTTP on port 443, bypassing port-based firewall rules. The MSI impersonates a Windows update and loads the RAT DLL directly into memory, leaving no obvious on-disk payload to catch.
- C2 is split across two legitimate services: Cloudflare Workers at is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers[.]dev handles SDP signaling to establish a WebRTC channel, then drops out entirely. All subsequent commands flow over a WebRTC DataChannel relayed through Twilio, so the attacker's real server IP never appears in traffic.
- The RAT binds only to 127.0.0[.]1. All external traffic originates from the browser process itself, launched headless with remote debugging enabled. CSP is bypassed via a CDP command and JavaScript injected into the browser handles every network operation. What a defender sees is a browser making HTTPS calls to Cloudflare and WebRTC to Twilio, both normal.
- Talos found msaRAT deployed between initial access and the Chaos encryptor, confirming it serves pre-encryption reconnaissance. Double encryption: DTLS from WebRTC plus ChaCha-Poly1305 over an ECDH-derived key means stripping DTLS still yields ciphertext.

item.title: Intelligence Insights: July 2026
item.description:
ClearFake holds 1st for the third straight month while CastleLoader debuts at 5th, using BYOI Python, finger.exe retrieval, and triple-layer encoded shellcode to drop RATs and infostealers via paste-and-run campaigns.
Key findings:
- ClearFake and KongTuke dominate the top 2 spots. KongTuke, a TDS abusing compromised WordPress sites, surged in June 2026 to levels not seen since November 2025. Observed chains use curl reaching out to .top domains via obfuscated paste-and-run commands for initial execution (T1204.002).
- CastleLoader infection chain starts with fake CAPTCHA pages on typosquatted sites like linkedall[.]org, golinked[.]net, and indeed-jobs[.]net, copying caret-obfuscated commands to clipboard. finger.exe retrieves batch commands from actor-controlled servers, a living-off-the-land retrieval technique worth hunting directly.
- BYOI evasion: CastleLoader downloads portable CPython or IronPython disguised as PDF files, extracts via tar.exe, and renames the interpreter to a random 12-18 digit filename under AppData\Local before execution, bypassing allowlists that rely on known interpreter paths.
- Shellcode delivery uses triple-layer encoding (Base64, zlib, UTF-32) with Cyrillic character substitution, then RC4-decrypts the final CastleLoader binary, which injects into python.exe. CastleLoader supports 14 launch methods including rundll32.exe, msiexec.exe, and powershell.exe, and detects VMware, VirtualBox, and Parallels via cpuid.

item.title: Email threat landscape: Q2 2026 trends and insights
item.description:
Microsoft's Q2 2026 email threat roundup: 7.6 billion phishing threats detected, Tycoon2FA volumes collapsed 92% post-disruption, and Teams-based vishing hit 10x the mid-2025 baseline.
Key findings:
- Tycoon2FA never recovered after March's DCU-led infrastructure action. Monthly volume fell from a 15.1M baseline to 1.2M by June, an 92% decline. The platform shifted to .RU TLD hosting after losing Cloudflare, but its share of CAPTCHA-gated phishing dropped from 76% peak to 12%, and QR code campaign share fell from 33% to 14%. No replacement PhaaS emerged at scale.
- Teams vishing is the sharpest growth vector this quarter: weekly malicious call attempts rose 80% since January 2026 and now run at nearly 10x the mid-2025 baseline. Attackers impersonate IT helpdesk, peak 14:00-20:00 UTC Mon-Fri, and increasingly use generic display names (52% in June) rather than obvious IT branding, likely blending with ClickFix-style lure themes.
- Two notable campaigns: a June 1 BEC wave hit 67,000 users across 42,000 orgs in under 3 hours using Python email.mime, Amazon SES API, DKIM-signed ecajovna[.]sk, and reply-to domains ilyff[.]com, j-gmails[.]com, x2mails[.]com. A June 14-15 campaign hit 107,000 users using nested EML, ICS calendar invite, a silent OAuth redirect through login.microsoftonline[.]com, and a BAT dropper (Financial_report.bat) pulling installer.exe from pixeldrain[.]com.

item.title: How Elasticsearch ES|QL COMPLETION turns noisy curl and wget rules into high-fidelity cloud security alerts
item.description:
ES|QL COMPLETION brings LLM triage inside individual Elastic detection rules, cutting curl/wget alert noise to near-zero before events ever reach an analyst queue.
Key findings:
- The technique targets T1105 (Ingress Tool Transfer). curl and wget are legitimate attacker tradecraft vectors, but cloud hosts use them constantly for CI, package pulls, and metadata calls. The approach parses the destination host from process.args (or process.command_line/process.title for schema-less invocations), applies a deterministic allow-list anchored to that parsed dest_host field, then passes surviving rows to an LLM via the COMPLETION command. Anchoring filters to the parsed field, not the raw command string, closes the substring-bypass gap where an expected domain appearing in a path accidentally suppresses a real alert.
- Secrets are redacted before COMPLETION runs: authorization headers, bearer tokens, API keys (x-api-key, x-amz-security-token, etc.), query-string credentials, URL-embedded auth, and JWT patterns (eyJ...) are all replaced inline. The prompt also instructs the model to treat all command and URL text as untrusted data to block prompt injection from attacker-controlled strings.
- In a seven-day QA run on Elastic's own cloud fleet, only three destinations survived deterministic filtering: cdn.playwright[.]dev (FP), 1.1[.]1.1 (FP), and an internal AWS IP flagged SUSPICIOUS. Zero analyst-facing alerts were generated.

item.title: TAG-195 Upgrades MaaS Ecosystem with Modular Tools
item.description:
TAG-195 ("Golden Chickens") expands its MaaS toolkit with four new malware families, including a modular implant architecture that loads capabilities on demand to shrink its detection footprint.
Key findings:
- TinyEgg is a lightweight initial-access backdoor handling host profiling, interactive shell, and persistence. ChonkyChicken builds on it with browser credential theft, session automation, credential-backed remote execution, and network recon. All four families share Run key persistence under a consistent value name, filename execution gating, string obfuscation, and payload delivery via a legitimate Windows binary.
- The modularized ChonkyChicken variant uses a controller-and-plugin design: a base implant requests and loads at least 14 capability modules on demand from attacker infrastructure. This deliberately reduces the static detection surface of the base implant while letting operators provision only the capabilities each intrusion needs.
- ChromEggscalator is a modified version of a publicly available Chrome encryption-bypass tool, repurposed as a browser credential theft helper inside the TAG-195 ecosystem.
- TAG-127 is an observed operator and customer, deploying TinyEgg via ClickFix-style campaigns: fake security verification pages trick victims into manually running malicious commands that pull and install payloads through a legitimate Windows system utility.

item.title: CVE-2026-16232: Critical Check Point SmartConsole Authentication Bypass Exploited in the Wild
item.description:

- CVE-2026-16232 (CWE-287) lets an unauthenticated remote attacker steal an application login token and authenticate to the Management Server with full admin rights. From there, an attacker can rewrite security policies across all managed gateways, alter admin accounts, manipulate VPN configs, and suppress logging. Compromise of the management plane is a force-multiplier: every firewall it controls is now suspect.
- Two companion CVEs ship in the same advisory: CVE-2026-62144 (CVSS 9.1), a management authentication bypass with privilege escalation, and CVE-2026-62145 (CVSS 7.5), a local privilege escalation in GaiaOS WebUI. Neither has known exploitation yet, but patch all three.
- Exploitation is confirmed pre-patch. Check Point published Jumbo Hotfixes on July 22. Fix versions: R82.10 Take 36+, R82 Take 118+, R81.20 Take 158+. Older branches (R81.10 and below) have no fix specified. Smart-1 Cloud is already protected.

- A second, unidentified threat actor operated concurrently in the same environment using DLL sideloading into legitimate Windows processes and custom backdoors, neither linked to Storm-2603. The layered activity from two actors obscured each other, complicating attribution and timeline reconstruction.
- The driver NSecKrnl.sys was loaded to tamper with memory and disable endpoint protections before subsequent activity, a classic BYOVD move that blind-spots EDR before the heavier tooling arrives.

item.title: Chaos ransomware's msaRAT: Living off the browser to build a covert C2 channel
item.description:
Chaos ransomware's msaRAT routes all C2 traffic through Chrome DevTools Protocol and WebRTC, making the RAT process itself invisible to network monitors while burying attacker comms inside legitimate browser activity.
Key findings:
- Delivered via curl.exe over plain HTTP on port 443 (bypassing port-only firewall rules) as update_ms.msi to C:\programdata\, which drops lib.dll directly into memory via a custom MSI action. The RAT exports a single function, RUN, and impersonates a Windows update in installer metadata.
- msaRAT launches Chrome or Edge in headless mode via CreateProcessW, injects JavaScript through CDP Runtime.evaluate after bypassing CSP, and signals the C2 through Cloudflare Workers endpoint is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers[.]dev. Twilio TURN (global.turn.twilio[.]com) relays all subsequent WebRTC DataChannel traffic, intentionally omitting ICE candidates so no P2P path forms and the attacker's real IP never appears in traffic.
- All network activity from the RAT process is limited to 127.0.0[.]1. External comms appear as browser-originated WebRTC, double-encrypted with ChaCha-Poly1305 over DTLS. The C2 IP 172.86.126[.]18 appears only in the initial MSI download.
- Hunt for headless browser processes (HeadlessChrome User-Agent) making WebRTC connections, MSI files writing DLLs to ProgramData, and curl.exe dropping installers. ClamAV sig Win.Downloader.ChaosRaas-10060321-0 and Snort rules SID 66839-66841 (v2), 301587 (v3) cover this.

item.description:

item.title: Intercepting Android WebView traffic under new certificate validity requirement by Chromium
item.description:
Burp Suite's 1-year proxy cert now fails Android WebView interception silently. Chromium's cert validity enforcement (CERT_VALIDITY_TOO_LONG, net_error -213) breaks TLS interception without any app-side pinning in place.
Key findings:
- Chromium in Android WebView enforces max cert lifetimes per CA/B Forum Baseline Requirements. Certs issued on or after March 15, 2026 must be 200 days or fewer. Burp generates a 365-day cert (notAfter one year out), which now hard-fails with SSL error code 1, net_error -213 in logcat. mitmproxy generates shorter-lived certs and intercepts cleanly.
- The check lives in CertVerifyProc::HasTooLongValidity inside libwebviewchromium.so. It applies to any leaf cert marked as issued by a known root, meaning your Burp CA cert alone does not exempt the generated leaf from the validity window check.
- Three workarounds, easiest first: (1) uninstall WebView updates via adb shell dumpsys webviewupdate to revert to version 113; (2) chain mitmproxy on port 9090 as upstream proxy to Burp on port 8080 using --mode upstream with --ssl-insecure; (3) Frida-hook both cert_verify_proc at offset 0x3e015f8 and CachingCertVerifier::Verify at 0x3e00068 in libwebviewchromium.so after disabling multiprocess via adb shell cmd webviewupdate disable-multiprocess.
Before your next Android WebView assessment, confirm your proxy cert lifetime with openssl x509 -noout -dates.

item.title: Defender's Remote Connections Blind Spot: FourToSixMapping
item.description:
A subtle KQL filter bug in Microsoft Defender XDR silently drops real C2 connections from DeviceNetworkEvents, creating a blind spot that survives purple team exercises and LLM-generated queries alike.
- The root cause: filtering DeviceNetworkEvents with RemoteIPType == "Public" misses connections logged as "FourToSixMapping", which appears when a Windows dual-stack socket maps an IPv4 address into IPv6 notation (e.g., ::ffff:8.8.8.8). Defender logs the RemoteIP in that format and tags it FourToSixMapping, not Public, so the event silently falls through the filter.
- KQL's ipv4_is_private() returns null on ::ffff:-prefixed addresses, not false. Null fails a where clause, so LLM-suggested "fix" queries that rely on ipv4_is_private(RemoteIP) to catch all external IPs also miss these events. Null is neither true nor false in KQL.
- The fix is a two-part normalization: include RemoteIPType in ("Public", "FourToSixMapping") in your where clause, then strip the prefix with replace_string(RemoteIP, "::ffff:", "") before passing the value to any IP evaluation function.
Audit your tenant now. Run the verification query from the article against a historical window to surface FourToSixMapping events with no corresponding Public entry for the same IP. Then patch every hunting and detection rule that uses RemoteIPType == "Public" as a standalone external-traffic filter, it is a silent false-negative factory.

item.description:
RenPy Loader chains MSBuild abuse and EtherHiding to deliver Amatera Stealer via fake games and cracks, with C2 addresses hidden on a public blockchain to evade takedown.
Key findings:
- Setup.exe drops a Ren'Py package containing XOR-encrypted files: config .GEg (key 81034149cd6f48c8821340204f92766e), encrypted ZIP j3lpTcg7kBRN.E3 (key A50YyY1), and anti-sandbox classes under data/python-packages/sys_config/. - The BAT sets MSBUILDENABLEALLPROPERTYFUNCTIONS=1 and calls MSBuild.exe against Nancy.csproj, which reflectively loads a trojanized Nancy .NET DLL via AppDomain.CurrentDomain.Load. The DLL (MD5: 29203ca123d51b1b33505a0813d360df) uses custom bytecode, API hashing, and multi-key XOR decryption across three embedded resources.
- GollopDevest.dll (810F257542018BE0FC62AF542D13D012) retrieves the encrypted C2 via an Ethereum JSON-RPC eth_call to bsc-dataseed.binance[.]org targeting contract 0x328a1fadff154290f0ce1389a4e633698cdfdaa7, a classic EtherHiding move. Final payloads download from 144.124.251[.]171, 195.63.140[.]33, and 78.40.196[.]252. Amatera Stealer C2: login.orbitalframework[.]cc.

item.title: Volexity Uncovers Zero-Day Campaign Targeting SonicWall VPN Appliances
item.description:

CVE-2026-15410, a code injection flaw in the AMC, then executes OS commands as root, completing the chain.

- Physical appliances carrying a default product_uuid (common across multiple customers' hardware) are also vulnerable to an authentication bypass that does not require either CVE, though UTA0533 did not use that path here.

item.title: CVE-2026-42533 Exposes Critical Pre-Auth nginx RCE Flaw
item.description:
CVE-2026-42533 is a critical pre-auth nginx RCE with a 10/10 lab exploitation rate, ASLR bypass included. Patch nginx now: 1.30.4, 1.31.3, and NGINX Plus R36 P7 or 37.0.3.1 are the fixed releases.
- CVE-2026-42533 affects nginx 0.9.6 through 1.30.3 stable and 1.31.2 mainline, plus NGINX Plus R33-R36 and 37.0.0.1-37.0.2.1. No auth, no client cert, no unusual setup required. PoC exists but is being withheld. Treat this as actively exploitable in the near term.
- Root cause: nginx's two-pass evaluation engine (LEN pass then VALUE pass) does not save and restore PCRE capture state. A regex map evaluation can overwrite shared capture data mid-flight, making LEN and VALUE disagree on buffer size, producing a heap overflow or an info leak. Chaining both gives reliable RCE with ASLR defeated.
- Vulnerable pattern: any config combining regex captures ($1 or named groups) with regex map variables in the same evaluation path. Affected directives include proxy_set_header, proxy_pass, rewrite, add_header, and root, across both HTTP and stream modules.
- The researcher released a static configuration scanner to flag vulnerable patterns without exploitation. Audit configs before patching where immediate upgrades are constrained.
Upgrade to 1.30.4 or 1.31.3 immediately. Run the released config scanner to identify exposed directive chains. Confirm NGINX Plus is on R36 P7 or 37.0.3.1. Prior CVE patches do not cover this flaw.

item.title: Top 5 Windows Events: Essential for Incident Response | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
Five Windows Event IDs that Invictus IR reaches for first on real-world incidents, covering lateral movement, persistence, authentication, and log tampering.
Key findings:
- Event ID 1149 (TerminalServices-RemoteConnectionManager Operational) fires early in an RDP session before authentication completes, making it ideal for hunting lateral movement via nested RDP chains. Combine with 4624 to confirm a full authenticated session and map source IPs and usernames.
- Event ID 4698 (Windows Security) records scheduled task creation, a persistence method favored by Sodinokibi/REvil and IcedID. Check task definitions under Task Scheduler folders and the registry for corroborating artifacts.
- Event ID 4624 (Windows Security) is the authentication anchor: logon type, source, and user in one record. Filter by compromised account to scope lateral movement and detect pass-the-hash (logon type 3 with NTLM).
- Event ID 7045 (Windows System/Security) logs new service installs and is a primary Cobalt Strike indicator. Ransomware groups rely heavily on CS, so this is one of the first checks on any Windows log.
- Event ID 1102 (Windows Security) means the audit log was cleared, almost never legitimate during an incident. Pivot on the user and timestamp; if logs feed a SIEM, the clear event itself becomes an investigation anchor.

item.title: AWS Cloud Native Incident Response: Part 2 | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
AWS Athena is a practical, low-friction triage tool for cloud IR: no indexing required, queries run directly against S3 logs, and cost control is built into how you write queries.
Key details:
- CloudTrail logs stored in S3 are the baseline artifact in most AWS environments. Athena, paired with AWS Glue for schema definition and partitioning, lets responders query them without standing up a SIEM. Glue partitions (region, year, month, day) are critical: queries scoped to a partition scan less data, run faster, and cost less.
- Supported log types for direct Athena loading include CloudTrail, S3 access logs, ELB access logs, VPC Flow Logs, and others with official DDL loading instructions. Each source needs its own DDL statement; the only field to update is the LOCATION pointing to the S3 path.
- Cost discipline matters during IR. Always use LIMIT 10 when exploring an unfamiliar table. Use the query result reuse feature (up to 7 days) when iterating on the same dataset, but disable it when hunting live activity.
- Nested fields require different query approaches. STRUCT fields (like useridentity) are accessible with dot notation. STRING fields like requestparameters require json_extract_scalar, for example: SELECT useridentity.type, json_extract_scalar(requestparameters, '$.roleSessionName') AS roleSessionName FROM cloudtrail_logs WHERE eventname = 'AssumeRole' ORDER BY eventtime DESC LIMIT 10.

item.title: Inside wp2shell: How Two WordPress Core Bugs Became a Critical RCE Chain
item.description:
WordPress Core RCE chain "wp2shell" (CVE-2026-63030 + CVE-2026-60137) enables unauthenticated attackers to reach full admin compromise and remote code execution. Emergency patches shipped July 17, 2026.
- CVE-2026-63030 is a REST API auth bypass in WP_REST_Server::serve_batch_request_v1(). Batch requests skip per-request permission checks, letting an unauthenticated caller access protected endpoints. Affects WordPress 6.9.0-6.9.4 and 7.0.0-7.0.1. Fixed in 6.9.5 and 7.0.2.
- CVE-2026-60137 is a SQL injection via the author__not_in parameter in WP_Query. Alone it required auth, limiting real-world risk. Once CVE-2026-63030 removes that barrier, the SQLi becomes reachable from the public internet with no credentials. Affects 6.8.0-6.8.5, 6.9.0-6.9.4, and 7.0.0-7.0.1.
- The chain ends in RCE through WordPress's own admin functionality: malicious plugin upload, theme file edit, or web shell drop. No exotic payload needed after db credentials are cracked offline and admin access is obtained.
- This hits WordPress Core, not a plugin, meaning every unpatched install is exposed regardless of plugin inventory.
Patch first (6.8.6, 6.9.5, or 7.0.2), then assume breach on any exposed instance. Hunt for new admin accounts, PHP files in upload dirs, modified Core files, and anomalous REST API batch requests in web server logs before and after the July 17 disclosure window.
